sources.title: Chapter 10 - Principles of Pipelining (Basic Computer Architecture)
sources.channel: IIT Delhi, Prof. Smruti R. Sarangi (freely distributed book chapter)
sources.note: the whole 92-page chapter was read: the pipeline idea and its performance, the five stages, pipeline registers, data/control/structural hazards, software solutions, interlocks and bubbles, forwarding paths and conditions, interrupts, the performance equation, branch prediction, multiple issue and out-of-order execution

sourceLine: Branch prediction, the 2-cycle penalty it hides, speculative instructions and the target buffer: Sarangi chapter 10, section 10.11.1 (English, read in full). The prediction strategies - static, 1-bit and 2-bit counters, BTB - and the penalty range: DSWallah Learn 'Pipeline Hazards & Stalls', romanised Hindi, translated (read in part).
title: Branch Prediction and Its Payoff
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Fixes
quickIdea: If the fetch unit guesses the branch direction it can keep fetching without waiting: a correct guess costs nothing and a wrong one costs the flush. Prediction therefore turns a fixed 2-cycle penalty into (1 - accuracy) x penalty on average.
remember: Static prediction: predict not taken (fetch p + 4, p + 8) or predict taken with the target computed early. Cheap, and right for loops only part of the time.
Dynamic prediction: a per-branch counter, 1-bit or 2-bit saturating, predicts the recent outcome; a branch target buffer caches the target so it is available at fetch.
Expected stall per branch = (1 - accuracy) x penalty, when a hit costs nothing and a miss costs the whole penalty.
CPI = 1 + branch fraction x expected stall per branch. The speed-up from adding a predictor is the ratio of the two CPIs when the clock is unchanged.
Prediction never removes the cost of a misprediction; it moves the cost from every branch to the fraction that is mispredicted, and speculative instructions must be discardable.

example.prompt: Processor X1 at 2 GHz has a 5-stage RISC pipeline with base CPI 1. In program P, 30 percent of instructions are branches and each branch stalls 2 cycles. X2 runs at the same clock and adds a branch predictor that removes the stall on a correct prediction and gives no saving and no extra penalty on a wrong one. With 80 percent accuracy, what is the speed-up of X2 over X1?
example.work: X1: CPI = 1 + 0.30 x 2 = 1.60. X2: a branch stalls 0 with probability 0.8 and 2 with probability 0.2, so the expected stall per branch is 0.4, and CPI = 1 + 0.30 x 0.4 = 1.12. Same clock and same program, so the speed-up is the CPI ratio 1.60 / 1.12 = 1.4286.
example.answer: 1.43 to two decimal places, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2022 Q.61 (accepted range 1.42 to 1.45).

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2022 Q.61 is the whole card in one question. The traps are to apply the accuracy to all instructions instead of to the branch fraction, and to assume a misprediction is cheaper than the original stall - the question explicitly forbids both.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: For the same program, what accuracy would X2 need to reach a speed-up of 1.6?
variations.why: It inverts the calculation and shows the diminishing return of accuracy.
variations.answer: CPI(X2) must be 1.60/1.6 = 1.00, so the branch term must vanish, which needs accuracy 1.0. Even at 95 percent accuracy the CPI is 1 + 0.30 x 0.05 x 2 = 1.03 and the speed-up only 1.55, so the last few percent of accuracy buy very little.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: A 2-bit saturating counter is at state 'weakly taken' and the branch is not taken twice. What does it predict on the next two occurrences?
variations.why: It tests the mechanism rather than the formula, which is how a theory question could ask it.
variations.answer: After one not-taken it moves to 'weakly not taken' but still predicts taken; after the second it moves to 'strongly not taken' and predicts not taken. The extra state is what makes a loop with one unusual exit iterate correctly instead of mispredicting twice.

trap.what: Multiplying the accuracy by the stall and subtracting from every instruction's cost.
trap.why: The saving applies only to branches, so the branch fraction must multiply the per-branch expected stall. Applying it to all instructions overstates the gain.
trap.counterexample: 2022 Q.61: applying 0.8 to all instructions would give a CPI near 0.68 and a speed-up above 2; the accepted speed-up is 1.43.

check.question: Forty percent of instructions are branches, a taken branch costs 3 cycles and the predictor is 75 percent accurate. What is the CPI?
check.explanation: The expected stall per branch is (1 - 0.75) x 3 = 0.75 cycles, and 40 percent of instructions are branches, so 0.3 cycles are added to the base cycle.
